newsitem.title: GERMANY: Issing - mark rate among prime indicators for Buba.
newsitem.headline: Issing - mark rate among prime indicators for Buba.

text.p: Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing said on Tuesday that the exchange rate of the mark was one of the most important indicators for the central bank in its setting of monetary policy.
"After money supply, the exchange rate is one of the most important indicators for the Bundesbank," Issing said in an interview with the weekly "Boerse-Online" magazine.
"The fact that the mark has weakened so fast and so significantly certainly gives us something to think about," he said.
But Issing added that there was no automatic link between the rate of the dollar versus the mark and interest rate decisions made by the German central bank.
The mark reached an eight-year low against the dollar earlier on Tuesday but had recovered and was trading at 1.8765 marks to the dollar by 1245 GMT.
Issing said the pace of movement in foreign exchange markets, rather than specific exchange rate levels, was of greater concern to the central bank.
"It is not the level, but the movement, the rapid depreciation of the mark, which is worrying us," he told the magazine.
A copy of the interview was released in advance of publication.

Issing stressed that the main task of the central bank was to defend the stability of the mark, adding that this obligation would remain in place right up until the planned launch of the single European currency set for January 1, 1999.
"I also think that defending the stability of national currencies is one of the key obligations in the interest of (European economic) and monetary union," Issing added.

Noting recent moves in German money markets, which have moved to price in higher interest rates in coming months, Issing told the magazine that the central bank could not steer its policy according to market expectations.
"The Bundesbank cannot orientate itself to such expectations," he said. "It must do what it considers to be right."

Turning to economic data, Issing said the current trend in German import prices, which in June reached their highest year-on-year level for six years, was going in the wrong direction, particularly given a recent fall in the cost of raw materials.
